content:
Draft outline from R005 — 25 slides, 40 minutes. Status: drafted for the instructor to rewrite in their own voice. Two slides (21, 22) and one note (25) carry placeholders that cannot be resolved until D01/D06/D08 and Q01/Q02/Q11/Q16 are settled. No image URLs are given — images are described in words and must be sourced and licensed by the instructor.

Timing

Part Slides Minutes
1. The loop 1–6 8
2. Three families 7–13 12
3. Lineage 14–16 6
4. Craft and the digital 17–20 9
5. This term 21–25 5

The argument in one line: the machine relocates risk, it does not remove it — set up in Part 1, named in Part 4 (Pye), and cashed out in the first assignment.

1 — Title: Bits to Atoms

Image: one object photographed twice — as a screen capture of its 3D model and as the finished physical object — side by side, same angle, same size on the slide.

Notes. Course, room, who you are. One sentence to open: for fifteen weeks you will move things back and forth across a single line — the line between a file and an object — and this course is about what happens at that line.

2 — Two objects, one question

Image: two objects of the same type side by side, uncaptioned — one visibly mass-produced (injection-moulded), one visibly handmade (thrown or hand-built).

Notes. Ask the room: which one took more skill? Let them argue for ninety seconds. Do not resolve it. Say: hold that thought, we come back to it at the end of today and again in week five. (This is the Pye seed; the whole lecture hangs off it.)

3 — The loop

Image: a four-node cycle — IDEA → FILE → MACHINE → OBJECT → back to IDEA. Thin arrows around; one thicker return arrow from OBJECT back to FILE.

Notes. The course in one diagram. Almost everything you learn lives on the arrows, not the nodes. The return arrow is the one beginners skip: the object tells you what the file got wrong. Making that return trip, on purpose and on the record, is most of what gets graded here.

4 — A file is not a picture of the thing

Image: the same simple form shown three ways — a vector outline; a triangulated mesh; a toolpath with visible stepover lines.

Notes. One form, three representations, three different machines. A vector is a set of paths for something to follow. A mesh is a skin with no inside. A toolpath already has a physical tool's width baked into it. Learning to tell at a glance which one you are looking at — and what it cannot express — is a real skill and you will have it by March.

5 — CAD → CAM → machine

Image: three stacked horizontal bands labelled CAD, CAM, MACHINE, with a short "what you decide here" line beneath each.

Notes. CAD is where you decide the form. CAM is where you decide how it gets made — orientation, order, which tool, how fast. The machine only executes. Nearly every beginner failure is a CAM decision made carelessly or not made at all. We spend real time in the middle band; most tutorials don't.

6 — The machine does not know what you mean

Image: a laser-cut part that failed because two lines which looked joined on screen were not — the part fell open. A real failure from your own shop is better than a clean illustration.

Notes. Tell the story behind the photograph. The machine has no model of your intent. Also worth separating now, because students conflate them all term: precision (repeatable), accuracy (correct), and right (what you actually wanted).

7 — Three families

Image: three simple icons — material added in layers; material cut away; material pushed into a shape.

Notes. Every fabrication process makes one of three moves: add, subtract, or deform. That's the whole taxonomy. Memorise it today — it is the vocabulary your first assignment is written in.

8 — Additive

Image: a raking-light macro photograph of FDM layer lines across a curved surface.

Notes. Build material up where you want it. Cheap in geometry — complexity is close to free — and expensive in time. The layer is a grain: the part is meaningfully weaker across layers than along them. You will feel this in week six when something snaps exactly where you didn't expect.

9 — Additive example: Nervous System, Kinematics Dress (2014)

Image: the dress on a form, plus a detail shot of the interlocking triangular panels and their hinges.

Notes. 2,279 triangular panels joined by 3,316 hinges, printed as a single piece in nylon by selective laser sintering, folded to fit inside the build volume and unfolded after printing. Acquired by MoMA. The point for us is not the technology: the build volume was a constraint, and folding was the design answer to it. Constraint-as-design-move is the recurring lesson of this course. (Nervous System's own project pages are on your reading list as a reference all term.)

10 — Subtractive

Image: a CNC-routed relief in plywood under raking light, tool stepover scallops clearly visible.

Notes. Start with stock and remove everything that isn't the object. Cheap in time relative to printing at scale, expensive in material and waste. The tool has a radius, a length, and a direction it can reach from — so an inside corner is never sharp, and an undercut is not reachable at all. In week nine that constraint is the design problem.

11 — Subtractive example: Barry X Ball, Masterworks

Image: one of Ball's milled stone portraits in onyx or Belgian black marble; alongside it, if you can source one, an image of the same piece at the milling stage with machine lines still on it.

Notes. Ball 3D-scans a historical sculpture, re-sculpts the scan digitally, then drives a computer-controlled stone-milling machine. The rough form emerges in about four days; finer milling runs for months. Then a team of three or four spends thousands of hours by hand removing the milling lines and polishing the surface to a mirror finish. Ask them to hold onto the ratio — four days of machine, thousands of hours of hand. Don't explain it yet. It is slide 19.

12 — Formative

Image: a vacuum former mid-pull, the heated sheet slumping down over a buck.

Notes. Neither add nor remove — deform. Casting, moulding, thermoforming, bending, stamping. The oldest of the three families, and the one where digital fabrication usually makes the tool rather than the object: you cut or print the mould, the buck, the jig. We get here in week eleven.

13 — Formative example: Lee Bontecou, vacuum-formed sculptures (late 1960s–early 1970s)

Image: one of the hanging vacuum-formed plastic works from the 1971 Castelli exhibition.

Notes. Vacuum-formed plastic, plastic tubing, frosted acrylic — biomorphic forms that look as though they should be heavy and aren't. Made with no digital tooling whatsoever. Say this out loud: the families are old; what is new is how the tooling gets made. It punctures the idea that digital fabrication is a new kind of making rather than a new kind of tool-making, and it sets up Part 3 honestly.

14 — So what is digital fabrication?

Image: text only, three lines, lots of space.

Notes. Offer a working definition and put it on the slide: fabrication in which the description of the object is machine-readable and machine-executable. That is all it means. But it follows that the object is copyable, versionable, sendable, and parameterisable — and those four words are the reason artists and designers care, not the machines themselves.

15 — Gershenfeld's claim

Image: a quiet slide with the article title, journal and year. No stock photography.

Notes. Neil Gershenfeld, "How to Make Almost Anything," Foreign Affairs, 2012 — your first reading, fifteen pages, open access, link on the site. His argument: personal fabrication will do to manufacturing roughly what the personal computer did to computing. Give them the one-sentence version, then set the actual task: find the sentence in it you don't believe, and bring it next week. (That is also the model for the reading responses.)

16 — The fab lab lineage

Image: a simple horizontal timeline — MIT's "How to Make (Almost) Anything" class → the first fab labs → the global network → Fab Academy.

Notes. The class you're sitting in descends from a class Gershenfeld taught at MIT for students who, as he tells it, just wanted to make stuff. Note what the model assumes: shared machines, documented process, published files. This course adopts all three — which is why documentation is graded and why your files get published at the end. The Fab Academy archive is public and is on your reading list as a reference.

17 — Back to slide 2

Image: the same two objects from slide 2, unchanged.

Notes. Reopen the argument from the top of class. Ask again, then give them the vocabulary they were missing.

18 — Pye: the workmanship of risk and of certainty

Image: text slide — the two terms, one short gloss each.

Notes. David Pye, The Nature and Art of Workmanship, 1968; you read the chapter in week five. Workmanship of risk: the outcome is not predetermined — it depends on care, judgement and dexterity exercised as you go. The potter's hand, the brush, the saw cut. Workmanship of certainty: the outcome is settled before making begins, by the jig, the mould, the machine. The printing press, the injection mould. The part people miss: this is a spectrum, not a ranking, and every made object mixes the two.

19 — Where is the risk in a machine-made object?

Image: the Barry X Ball milling image again, now annotated — "certainty" over the milled stage, "risk" over the hand-finishing.

Notes. The mill is certainty. Three thousand hours of hand polishing is risk. Then turn it on the room: in a laser-cut piece, where is the risk? Push until they get past "the machine does it all" — the material choice, the decision to run a test cut or skip it, the tolerance you guessed at, the assembly, the finish, knowing when it's done. The machine relocates risk; it does not delete it. This is the single most useful idea in the course, and it is exactly what the first assignment asks them to find.

20 — McCullough: the practiced digital hand

Image: text slide. Describe the book plainly — author, title, publisher, year.

Notes. Malcolm McCullough, Abstracting Craft: The Practiced Digital Hand (MIT Press, 1996), argues the other side: that working digitally can itself be craft — that there is skilled, practiced, felt work to be done in a medium made of symbols. We read chapter one in week five, after you have made something and have an opinion worth having. Leave Pye and McCullough in tension; don't resolve it for them today or in week five.

21 — What we make this term

Image: a fifteen-week strip in four bands, labelled by what students make rather than by machine names.

PLACEHOLDER — do not finalise. The process order is a hypothesis, not a plan: D01 (which processes, in what order) and D08 (CNC for everyone vs. demo + optional) are open and depend on Q01, Q02 and Q11. Present this as "roughly" and say out loud that the shop tour may change it — students respond well to being told the truth about a course still being built.

Notes. Roughly: getting three-dimensional form out of flat material; then building up in three dimensions; then working at scale and in series; then a self-directed final project. Short exercises between, two projects, and a final. Say the shape; don't promise the machines until after the tour.

22 — What you hand in

Image: a simple table — exercises · projects · documentation · reading responses · critique.

PLACEHOLDER — no percentages on this slide yet. Weights follow D06, and A14 (precedent presentation) currently has no weight set. Show the categories on day one and point at the syllabus for numbers.

Notes. Emphasise two that students underrate: the documentation portfolio is a graded deliverable, not an afterthought, and critique attendance is graded because a crit with half the room missing doesn't work.

23 — Two rules for the term

Image: text, two lines — "Test first." / "Document as you go."

Notes. Test cut before the real cut, every time, no exceptions — you will hear this until it is annoying and then one day it will save a project. And documentation is not something you do at the end: the portfolio in April is assembled from what you record in January. Photograph the failures. Especially the failures.

24 — Your first assignment

Image: an exploded-view or cutaway drawing of an ordinary manufactured object.

Notes. A01, Object autopsy. Bring an object you own. Diagram how it was made — processes, materials, joints, tolerances, finish. Name the families from slide 7. Find the certainty and find the risk. Three slides plus a paragraph on what surprised you, due next week; worksheet on the site.

25 — Next: shop tour and safety

Image: a photograph of the shop taken from the doorway, machines visible.

Notes. Hand over to the lab tech. Closed shoes, tied-back hair, nothing loose at the wrists. Nobody touches a machine before certification.

PLACEHOLDER — certification wording. The specific requirement, who runs it and when depends on Q16 and the shop's own rules; confirm with the facilities manager before this slide is finalised. Do not state a certification process on day one that turns out to be wrong.

Images to source

None of these are supplied as URLs and none should be invented. Eleven slides need a real image (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 24, 25); slides 3, 5, 7 need diagrams you draw; the rest are text.

Two are already in the course's own reading list and are the natural first stop for slides 9 and 16 (Nervous System's studio project pages; the Fab Academy archive). Slides 6 and 25 should be your own photographs — a real failure from this shop and this room's actual door — and they will be the two slides students remember. Everything else needs permission or a licence checked before the deck is public; a follow-up request has been opened to do that sourcing.
